title: Rabi'a of Basra
hookLine: Rabi'a of Basra, who prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven or fear of hell

cards: Why does anyone do good? For love. For the thanks, the good feeling, the reputation.
For fear of what happens if they don't. Usually it's a mix. Basra, in southern Iraq, in the generations after the Prophet.
People tell a story about a woman walking through the city with a torch in one hand and a bucket of water in the other. Someone stops her and asks what she's doing.

teach.h: A STORY: FIRE ON PARADISE, WATER ON HELL.
teach.b: She is Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya, Rabi'a of Basra, who died, tradition says, around the year 800.

In the story, she answers: I want to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both veils are gone, and people worship God not out of hope for reward or fear of punishment, but for His own sake.
It's a story people tell, not a sourced report. And the sources need some honesty.
Rabi'a left no writings. Much of what's told about her comes from writers who lived long after her, above all the Persian poet Farid al-Din 'Attar, writing centuries later.
Tradition says she was born poor, was enslaved as a girl, and was freed because her master saw a light over her while she prayed at night. Historians can't confirm those details.
What's consistent across the sources is the center of her teaching: love, mahabbah.

A prayer attributed to her in the old Sufi books runs roughly like this: if I worship You out of fear of hell, then burn me in it; if I worship You hoping for paradise, then shut me out of it; but if I worship You for Your own sake, then don't hold back Your eternal beauty from me.
The Qur'an speaks of people whom God loves and who love Him. Rabi'a, as she's remembered, made that love the center. She isn't saying heaven and hell don't matter; Muslims hold that they're real.

how: Sufis honor Rabi'a of Basra for placing pure love of God at the center of the path, and her attributed sayings are still taught in Sufi circles and recited in poetry.

o: fear of God's punishment in hell
love, above all the love of God

p: to put out the fires of hell

s: Rabi'a left behind books of her teaching

much of what's told about her was written centuries after she died

games.q: you meet a woman in Basra carrying a torch and a bucket of water. you ask why. what does she say, in the story?
o: to light the mosque and wash its floor.
to burn paradise and put out hell, so people love God for His own sake.
to help a neighbor whose house is on fire.
games.why: in the story she wants both veils gone, reward and fear, so people worship God for Himself. it's told, not sourced.

practice: Think of a small kindness nobody will ever know was you: paying for a stranger's coffee, picking up litter on a street you'll never walk again, praying for someone who doesn't know you exist.
Choose it, notice the part of you that wants credit, and just smile at it. If you pray, you can ask to love for its own sake.

wordCard.voice: Mahabbah. Love — the center of Rabi'a of Basra's teaching, worshiping God for His own sake alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: love. Rabi'a is remembered for putting love of God at the center of the Sufi path.

carryVoice: Your line: love for its own sake. Not for the garden, and not for fear of the fire. Until tomorrow, then.
